l: Eukaryote

The eukaryotes are <color=#3366CC>cellular</color> <color=#3366CC>organisms</color> of the <color=#3366CC>domain</color> Eukaryota or Eukarya, which have a distinct <color=#3366CC>cell nucleus</color> (formed
by a <color=#3366CC>nuclear membrane</color>), <color=#3366CC>membrane-bound organelles</color> and organization supported by a <color=#3366CC>cytoskeleton</color>. Extant

eukaryotes are traditionally grouped into four <color=#3366CC>kingdoms</color>, namely <color=#3366CC>animals</color>, <color=#3366CC>plants</color>, <color=#3366CC>fungi</color> and <color=#3366CC>protists</color>.

"Protists" are a basal paraphyletic group that includes all <color=#3366CC>algae</color>, <color=#3366CC>amoebae</color>, <color=#3366CC>flagellates</color> and <color=#3366CC>ciliates</color>; however, this is now
considered a wastebasket taxon and has been replaced with newer classifications that better represent the <color=#3366CC>phylogeny</color>
of these organisms. As part of the prevailing three-domain system, eukaryotes constitute a major group of organisms
alongside the two domains of <color=#3366CC>prokaryotes</color>: <color=#3366CC>Bacteria</color> and <color=#3366CC>Archaea</color>.

<color=#3366CC>Cladistically</color>, eukaryotes emerged within the <color=#3366CC>archaeal</color> <color=#3366CC>phylum</color> <color=#3366CC>Promethearchaeota</color>, colloquially also known as "<color=#3366CC>Asgard</color>
<color=#3366CC>archaea</color>". Ignoring <color=#3366CC>mitochondrial DNA</color> (which comes from a bacterial lineage rather than an archaeal one), this would
imply only two domains of life, Bacteria and Archaea, with eukaryotes incorporated as a <color=#3366CC>clade</color> under the Archaea.
Eukaryotes first emerged during the <color=#3366CC>Paleoproterozoic</color>, and the leading <color=#3366CC>evolutionary</color> theory is that they were the result of
a metabolically <color=#3366CC>mutualistic</color> <color=#3366CC>symbiogenesis</color> between an anaerobic <color=#3366CC>Promethearchaeota</color> archaeon and an endosymbiont
aerobic alphaproteobacterium (i.e. proto-mitochondrion) in response to the oxidative stress following the <color=#3366CC>Great</color>
<color=#3366CC>Oxygenation Event</color>. A second symbiogenetic event between an eukaryotic <color=#3366CC>host</color> (a protist) and a beta-<color=#3366CC>cyanobacteria</color>
endosymbiont during the <color=#3366CC>Mesoproterozoic</color> led to the latter becoming <color=#3366CC>chloroplasts</color>, and resulted in the evolution of the

<color=#3366CC>photosynthetic</color> clade <color=#3366CC>Archaeplastida</color>, which includes all <color=#3366CC>green algae</color>, <color=#3366CC>red algae</color>, <color=#3366CC>glaucophytes</color> and <color=#3366CC>land plants</color>.
Eukaryotes can be unicellular or multicellular, and their cell sizes are significantly (hundreds of times) larger than
prokaryotes. They have <color=#3366CC>biomembranes</color> enclosing their nucleus and <color=#3366CC>organelles</color> such as the <color=#3366CC>endoplasmic reticulum</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Golgi apparatus</color>, <color=#3366CC>ribosome</color>, <color=#3366CC>vacuole</color> and <color=#3366CC>lysosome</color>, as well as endosymbiont-derived organelles (which are bound by

two or more layers of membrane) such as <color=#3366CC>mitochondria</color> and various <color=#3366CC>plastids</color>. Eukaryotes can <color=#3366CC>reproduce</color> both <color=#3366CC>asexually</color>

through <color=#3366CC>mitosis</color>, and <color=#3366CC>sexually</color> through <color=#3366CC>meiosis</color> and <color=#3366CC>gamete</color> fusion (<color=#3366CC>fertilization</color>). Due to their larger size and more
complex cellular architecture, eukaryotes are capable of morphogenesis and phagocytosis, which enables microscopic
<color=#3366CC>predation</color> of other unicellular organisms. Multicellularity in some eukaryotes led to <color=#3366CC>cell differentiation</color> and functional
specialization, which led to the formation of various <color=#3366CC>organs</color> and <color=#3366CC>tissues</color> and the development of <color=#3366CC>organ systems</color>.
Eukaryotes represent only a small minority of the total number of organisms on Earth, but due to their generally much
larger sizes, their collective global biomass is much greater than that of prokaryotes.
Etymology
The word eukaryote is derived from the <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> words "eu" meaning "true" or "good" and "karyon" meaning "nut" or
"kernel", referring to the <color=#3366CC>nucleus</color> of a <color=#3366CC>cell</color>.
Diversity
Eukaryotes are <color=#3366CC>organisms</color> that range from microscopic single <color=#3366CC>cells</color>, such as picozoans under 3 micrometers across, to

<color=#3366CC>animals</color> like the <color=#3366CC>blue whale</color>, weighing up to 190 <color=#3366CC>tonnes</color> and measuring up to 33.6 meter long, or <color=#3366CC>plants</color> like the <color=#3366CC>coast</color>
<color=#3366CC>redwood</color>, up to 120 meter tall. Many eukaryotes are unicellular; the informal grouping called <color=#3366CC>protists</color> includes many of
these, with some multicellular forms like the giant kelp up to 200 ft long. The multicellular eukaryotes include the
animals, plants, and <color=#3366CC>fungi</color>, but again, these groups too contain many unicellular <color=#3366CC>species</color>. Eukaryotic cells are typically
much larger than those of <color=#3366CC>prokaryotes</color>—the <color=#3366CC>bacteria</color> and the <color=#3366CC>archaea</color>—having a volume of around 10,000 times
greater. Eukaryotes represent a small minority of the number of <color=#3366CC>organisms</color>, but, as many of them are much larger, their
collective global biomass (468 gigatons) is far larger than that of prokaryotes (77 gigatons), with plants alone
accounting for over 81% of the total biomass of <color=#3366CC>Earth</color>.
The eukaryotes are a diverse lineage, consisting mainly of <color=#3366CC>microscopic organisms</color>. Multicellularity in some form has
<color=#3366CC>evolved independently</color> at least 25 times within the eukaryotes. Complex multicellular organisms, not counting the
aggregation of amoebae to form <color=#3366CC>slime molds</color>, have evolved within only six eukaryotic lineages: <color=#3366CC>animals</color>,

<color=#3366CC>symbiomycotan fungi</color>, <color=#3366CC>brown algae</color>, <color=#3366CC>red algae</color>, <color=#3366CC>green algae</color>, and <color=#3366CC>land plants</color>. Eukaryotes are grouped by genomic
similarities, so that groups often lack visible shared characteristics.
Distinguishing features
Nucleus
The defining feature of eukaryotes is their membrane-bound <color=#3366CC>nucleus</color>, distinguishing them from <color=#3366CC>prokaryotes</color> that lack a
nucleus. Eukaryotic cells are often much larger and contain more genetic information than bacterial cells. This genetic
information is divided into multiple linear molecules of <color=#3366CC>DNA</color> called <color=#3366CC>chromosomes</color>, which are contained inside the
nucleus.
Chromosomes are packaged into a highly organized structure called <color=#3366CC>chromatin</color> by histone proteins. Chromatin is
further organized by other DNA binding proteins, which regulate the folded shape of chromosomes. During <color=#3366CC>mitotic</color>
<color=#3366CC>division</color>, these chromosomes compacted and separated into two matching sets by a microtubular spindle.
Internal membranes
Eukaryote cells include a variety of membrane-bound structures, together forming the endomembrane system. Simple
compartments, called <color=#3366CC>vesicles</color> and <color=#3366CC>vacuoles</color>, can form by budding off other membranes. Many cells ingest food and
other materials through a process of <color=#3366CC>endocytosis</color>, where the outer membrane invaginates and then pinches off to form
a vesicle. Some cell products can leave in a vesicle through <color=#3366CC>exocytosis</color>.
The nucleus is surrounded by a double membrane known as the <color=#3366CC>nuclear envelope</color>, with nuclear pores that allow
material to move in and out. Various tube- and sheet-like extensions of the nuclear membrane form the <color=#3366CC>endoplasmic</color>
<color=#3366CC>reticulum</color>, which is involved in <color=#3366CC>protein transport</color> and maturation. It includes the rough endoplasmic reticulum, covered in
<color=#3366CC>ribosomes</color> which synthesize proteins; these enter the interior space or lumen. Subsequently, they generally enter
vesicles, which bud off from the smooth endoplasmic reticulum. In most eukaryotes, these protein-carrying vesicles are
released and their contents further modified in stacks of flattened vesicles (cisternae), the <color=#3366CC>Golgi apparatus</color>.
Vesicles may be specialized; for instance, <color=#3366CC>lysosomes</color> contain digestive enzymes that break down <color=#3366CC>biomolecules</color> in the
cytoplasm.
Mitochondria
Mitochondria are organelles in eukaryotic cells. The mitochondrion is commonly called "the powerhouse of the cell", for
its function providing energy by oxidizing sugars or fats to produce the energy-storing molecule <color=#3366CC>ATP</color>. Mitochondria
have two surrounding <color=#3366CC>membranes</color>, each a <color=#3366CC>phospholipid bilayer</color>, the inner of which is folded into invaginations called
cristae where <color=#3366CC>aerobic respiration</color> takes place.
Mitochondria contain <color=#3366CC>their own DNA</color>, which is circular like bacterial DNA, from which it originated, and which encodes
<color=#3366CC>rRNA</color> and <color=#3366CC>tRNA</color> genes that produce RNA which is closer in structure to bacterial RNA than to eukaryote RNA.
Some eukaryotes, such as the metamonads Giardia and Trichomonas, and the amoebozoan Pelomyxa, appear to lack
mitochondria, but all contain mitochondrion-derived organelles, like hydrogenosomes or mitosomes, having lost their
mitochondria secondarily. They obtain energy by enzymatic action in the cytoplasm. It is thought that mitochondria
developed from <color=#3366CC>prokaryotic</color> cells which became endosymbionts living inside eukaryotes.
Plastids
Plants and various groups of <color=#3366CC>algae</color> have plastids as well as mitochondria. Plastids, like mitochondria, have <color=#3366CC>their own</color>
<color=#3366CC>DNA</color> and are developed from endosymbionts, in this case <color=#3366CC>cyanobacteria</color>. They usually take the form of <color=#3366CC>chloroplasts</color>
which, like cyanobacteria, contain <color=#3366CC>chlorophyll</color> and produce organic compounds (such as <color=#3366CC>glucose</color>) through
<color=#3366CC>photosynthesis</color>. Others are involved in storing food. Although plastids probably had a single origin, not all
plastid-containing groups are closely related. Instead, some eukaryotes have obtained them from other eukaryotes
through <color=#3366CC>secondary endosymbiosis</color> or ingestion. The capture and sequestering of photosynthetic cells and chloroplasts,
kleptoplasty, occurs in many types of modern eukaryotic organisms.
Cytoskeletal structures
The cytoskeleton provides stiffening structure and points of attachment for motor structures that enable the cell to
move, change shape, or transport materials. The motor structures are <color=#3366CC>microfilaments</color> of <color=#3366CC>actin</color> and actin-binding
proteins. These include -actinin, fimbrin, and filamin in submembranous cortical layers and bundles. Motor proteins of
microtubules, dynein and kinesin, and <color=#3366CC>myosin</color> of actin filaments, make the network dynamic.
Many eukaryotes have long slender motile cytoplasmic projections, called <color=#3366CC>flagella</color>, or multiple shorter structures called
<color=#3366CC>cilia</color>. These organelles are variously involved in movement, feeding, and sensation. They are composed mainly of
tubulin, and are entirely distinct from prokaryotic flagella. They are supported by a bundle of <color=#3366CC>microtubules</color> arising from a
<color=#3366CC>centriole</color>, characteristically arranged as nine doublets surrounding two singlets. Flagella may have hairs
(mastigonemes), as in many <color=#3366CC>stramenopiles</color>. Their interior is continuous with the cell's <color=#3366CC>cytoplasm</color>.
Centrioles are often present, even in cells and groups that do not have flagella, but <color=#3366CC>conifers</color> and <color=#3366CC>flowering plants</color> have
neither. They generally occur in groups that give rise to various microtubular roots. These form a primary component of
the cytoskeleton, and are often assembled over the course of several cell divisions, with one flagellum retained from
the parent and the other derived from it. Centrioles produce the spindle during nuclear division.
Cell wall
The cells of plants, algae, fungi and most <color=#3366CC>chromalveolates</color>, but not animals, are surrounded by a cell wall. This is a
layer outside the <color=#3366CC>cell membrane</color>, providing the cell with structural support, protection, and a filtering mechanism. The
cell wall also prevents over-expansion when water enters the cell.

The major <color=#3366CC>polysaccharides</color> making up the primary cell wall of <color=#3366CC>land plants</color> are <color=#3366CC>cellulose</color>, hemicellulose, and <color=#3366CC>pectin</color>. The
cellulose microfibrils are linked together with hemicellulose, embedded in a pectin matrix. The most common
hemicellulose in the primary cell wall is xyloglucan.
Sexual reproduction
Eukaryotes have a life cycle that involves <color=#3366CC>sexual reproduction</color>, alternating between a <color=#3366CC>haploid</color> phase, where only one
copy of each chromosome is present in each cell, and a <color=#3366CC>diploid</color> phase, with two copies of each chromosome in each
cell. The diploid phase is formed by fusion of two haploid gametes, such as <color=#3366CC>eggs</color> and <color=#3366CC>spermatozoa</color>, to form a <color=#3366CC>zygote</color>;
this may grow into a body, with its cells dividing by <color=#3366CC>mitosis</color>, and at some stage produce haploid gametes through
<color=#3366CC>meiosis</color>, a division that reduces the number of chromosomes and creates genetic variability. There is considerable
variation in this pattern. Plants have both <color=#3366CC>haploid and diploid multicellular phases</color>. Eukaryotes have lower metabolic
rates and longer generation times than prokaryotes, because they are larger and therefore have a smaller surface area
to volume ratio.
The <color=#3366CC>evolution of sexual reproduction</color> may be a primordial characteristic of eukaryotes. Based on a phylogenetic
analysis, Dacks and Roger have proposed that facultative sex was present in the group's common ancestor. A core set
of genes that function in meiosis is present in both <color=#3366CC>Trichomonas vaginalis</color> and <color=#3366CC>Giardia intestinalis</color>, two organisms
previously thought to be asexual. Since these two species are descendants of lineages that diverged early from the
eukaryotic evolutionary tree, core meiotic genes, and hence sex, were likely present in the common ancestor of
eukaryotes. Species once thought to be asexual, such as Leishmania parasites, have a sexual cycle. Amoebae,
previously regarded as asexual, may be anciently sexual; while present-day asexual groups could have arisen recently.
Biochemistry
Eukaryotes differ from prokaryotes in multiple ways, with unique biochemical pathways such as sterane synthesis. The
eukaryotic signature <color=#3366CC>proteins</color> have no homology to proteins in other domains of life, but appear to be universal among
eukaryotes. They include the proteins of the cytoskeleton, the complex <color=#3366CC>transcription</color> machinery, the membrane-sorting
systems, the nuclear pore, and some <color=#3366CC>enzymes</color> in the biochemical pathways.
Evolution
History of classification

In <color=#3366CC>antiquity</color>, the two lineages of <color=#3366CC>animals</color> and <color=#3366CC>plants</color> were recognized by <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color> and <color=#3366CC>Theophrastus</color>. The lineages were
given the <color=#3366CC>taxonomic rank</color> of kingdom by <color=#3366CC>Linnaeus</color> in the 18th century. Though he included the <color=#3366CC>fungi</color> with plants with
some reservations, it was later realized that they are quite distinct and warrant a separate kingdom. The various
single-cell eukaryotes were originally placed with plants or animals when they became known. In 1818, the German
biologist Georg A. Goldfuss coined the word <color=#3366CC>Protozoa</color> to refer to organisms such as <color=#3366CC>ciliates</color>, and this group was
expanded until <color=#3366CC>Ernst Haeckel</color> made it a kingdom encompassing all single-celled eukaryotes, the <color=#3366CC>Protista</color>, in 1866. The
eukaryotes thus came to be seen as four kingdoms:
• Kingdom <color=#3366CC>Protista</color>
• Kingdom <color=#3366CC>Plantae</color>
• Kingdom <color=#3366CC>Fungi</color>
• Kingdom <color=#3366CC>Animalia</color>
The protists were at that time thought to be "primitive forms", and thus an evolutionary grade, united by their primitive
unicellular nature. Understanding of the oldest branchings in the tree of life only developed substantially with DNA
sequencing, leading to a system of <color=#3366CC>domains</color> rather than kingdoms as top level rank being put forward by <color=#3366CC>Carl Woese</color>,
Otto Kandler, and Mark Wheelis in 1990, uniting all the eukaryote kingdoms in the domain "Eucarya", stating, however,
that eukaryotes' will continue to be an acceptable common synonym". In 1996, the evolutionary biologist <color=#3366CC>Lynn Margulis</color>
proposed to replace kingdoms and domains with "inclusive" names to create a "symbiosis-based phylogeny", giving the
description "Eukarya (symbiosis-derived nucleated organisms)".
Phylogeny
By the early 21st century, a rough consensus started to emerge from phylogenomic studies. The majority of eukaryotes
can be placed in one of two large clades dubbed Amorphea (similar in composition to the unikont hypothesis) and the
<color=#3366CC>Diphoda</color> (formerly bikonts), which includes plants and most algal lineages. A third major grouping, the <color=#3366CC>Excavata</color>, has
been abandoned as a formal group as it was found to be paraphyletic. The proposed phylogeny below includes two
groups of excavates (Discoba and Metamonada), and incorporates the 2021 proposal that picozoans are close
relatives of rhodophytes. The Provora are a group of microbial predators discovered in 2022. <color=#3366CC>TSAR</color> is a possible clade
that would contain Telonemia and the <color=#3366CC>SAR supergroup</color>.
Origin of eukaryotes
The origin of the eukaryotic cell, or eukaryogenesis, is a milestone in the evolution of life, since eukaryotes include all
complex cells and almost all multicellular organisms. The last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) is the hypothetical
origin of all living eukaryotes, and was most likely a <color=#3366CC>biological population</color>, not a single individual. The LECA is believed
to have been a protist with a nucleus, at least one <color=#3366CC>centriole</color> and <color=#3366CC>flagellum</color>, facultatively aerobic mitochondria, sex

(<color=#3366CC>meiosis</color> and <color=#3366CC>syngamy</color>), a dormant <color=#3366CC>cyst</color> with a cell wall of <color=#3366CC>chitin</color> or <color=#3366CC>cellulose</color>, and <color=#3366CC>peroxisomes</color>.
An <color=#3366CC>endosymbiotic union</color> between a motile anaerobic archaean and an aerobic alphaproteobacterium gave rise to the
LECA and all eukaryotes with <color=#3366CC>mitochondria</color>. A second, much later endosymbiosis with a cyanobacterium gave rise to
the ancestor of plants, with <color=#3366CC>chloroplasts</color>.
The presence of eukaryotic biomarkers in archaea points towards an archaeal origin, except for mitochondrial DNA,
which is bacterial in origin. The genomes of Promethearchaeota archaea have plenty of <color=#3366CC>eukaryotic signature protein</color>
genes, which play a crucial role in the development of the <color=#3366CC>cytoskeleton</color> and complex cellular structures characteristic of
eukaryotes. In 2022, cryo-electron tomography demonstrated that Promethearchaeota archaea have a complex
<color=#3366CC>actin</color>-based cytoskeleton, providing the first direct visual evidence of the archaeal ancestry of eukaryotes.
Fossils
The timing of the origin of eukaryotes is hard to determine. Multiple different fossils that may be early eukaryotes have
been suggested, but remain contested. Fossils that are clearly related to modern groups start appearing an estimated
1.2 billion years ago, in the form of <color=#3366CC>red algae</color>, though fossilized Vindhyan <color=#3366CC>filamentous algae</color> have been suggested to be
as much as 1.6 to 1.7 billion years old, rather than <color=#3366CC>Cambrian</color> as previously thought. A 2026 study suggests that early
fossil eukaryotes (1.75-1.4 Gya) may have been <color=#3366CC>benthic</color> aerobes, living on the bottom of oxygenated waters, and may
not have colonised <color=#3366CC>planktonic</color> environments until much later, after 1 Gya.
Fossils from the Ruyang Group of China, dating to approximately 1.8-1.6 billion years ago, may be the oldest known
eukaryotes. One possible earliest multicellular eukaryote fossil is Qingshania magnifica from North China, which lived
1.635 billion years ago. This would suggest that the crown group eukaryotes originated in the late <color=#3366CC>Paleoproterozoic</color>
(Statherian). Other early unicellular eukaryotes, Tappania plana, Shuiyousphaeridium macroreticulatum, Dictyosphaera
macroreticulata, Germinosphaera alveolata, and Valeria lophostriata from North China, lived approximately 1.65 billion
years ago.
Some acritarchs are known from at least 1.65 billion years ago, and a fossil, Grypania, which may be an alga, is as
much as 2.1 billion years old. The <color=#3366CC>"problematic"</color> fossil Diskagma has been found in <color=#3366CC>paleosols</color> 2.2 billion years old. The
<color=#3366CC>Neoarchean</color> fossil Thuchomyces shares some similarities with fungi. It especially resembles the problematic fossil
Diskagma, with hyphae and multiple differentiated layers. However, it is over 600 million years older than all other
possible eukaryotes, and many of its "eukaryote features" are not specific to the clade, meaning it is almost certainly a
microbial mat instead.
Structures proposed to represent "large colonial organisms" have been found in the <color=#3366CC>black shales</color> of the
<color=#3366CC>Palaeoproterozoic</color> such as the Francevillian B Formation, in <color=#3366CC>Gabon</color>, dubbed the "Francevillian biota" which is dated at
2.1 billion years old. However, the status of these structures as fossils is contested, with other authors suggesting that
they might represent pseudofossils.
The presence of steranes, eukaryotic-specific biomarkers, in <color=#3366CC>Australian</color> <color=#3366CC>shales</color> previously indicated that eukaryotes
were present in these rocks dated at 2.7 billion years old, but these Archaean biomarkers have been rebutted as later
contaminants. The oldest valid biomarker records are only around 800 million years old. In contrast, a molecular clock
analysis suggests the emergence of sterol biosynthesis as early as 2.3 billion years ago. The nature of steranes as
eukaryotic biomarkers is further complicated by the production of sterols by some bacteria.
Whenever their origins, eukaryotes may not have become ecologically dominant until much later; a massive increase in
the <color=#3366CC>zinc composition</color> of marine sediments 800 Ma has been attributed to the rise of substantial populations of
eukaryotes, which preferentially consume and incorporate <color=#3366CC>zinc</color> relative to prokaryotes, approximately a billion years
after their origin (at the latest).
Middle East
The Middle East is a geopolitical region that is generally defined as encompassing all of <color=#3366CC>West Asia</color> except for the
<color=#3366CC>Caucasus</color> and including African Egypt and <color=#3366CC>European Turkey</color>. It roughly corresponds with what was historically referred
to in <color=#3366CC>Western Europe</color> as the <color=#3366CC>Near East</color>, which was juxtaposed with the <color=#3366CC>Far East</color>. Unlike West Asia's adherence to
continental boundaries, the Middle East is demarcated by following <color=#3366CC>political borders</color>. Since the early 20th century, the
term "Middle East" has grown increasingly prominent in international discourse, although it is often prone to causing
confusion or disagreement on account of vague and changing definitions of what countries and regions it spans. The
related terms "<color=#3366CC>Middle East and North Africa</color>" and "Greater Middle East" denote other existing concepts of the region
that involve extending the "Middle East" to incorporate most <color=#3366CC>Muslim-majority countries</color>.
Today, the bulk of Middle Eastern countries (13 out of 18) are part of the <color=#3366CC>Arab world</color>. The three most populous Middle

Eastern countries are <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>, <color=#3366CC>Iran</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Turkey</color>, while <color=#3366CC>Saudi Arabia</color> is the largest Middle Eastern country by area. <color=#3366CC>Arabs</color>
are the most widespread ethnic group in the region, followed by Turks, <color=#3366CC>Persians</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kurds</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jews</color>, and Assyrians.
Significant geographical features or regions that constitute the Middle East are the <color=#3366CC>Arabian Peninsula</color>, <color=#3366CC>Anatolia</color>, the
<color=#3366CC>Levant</color> and <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color> (together comprising the <color=#3366CC>Fertile Crescent</color>), and the <color=#3366CC>Iranian plateau</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>history of the Middle East</color> is among the richest ever recorded as it was the first region to be <color=#3366CC>settled by modern</color>
<color=#3366CC>humans outside of Africa</color> and the first region in which <color=#3366CC>writing systems were developed</color>. Situated at the intersection of
<color=#3366CC>Africa, Europe, and Asia</color>, the Middle East was home to several <color=#3366CC>cradles of civilization</color> and has been recognized by both
local and foreign populations as a region of great strategic importance for millennia. All of the core <color=#3366CC>Abrahamic religions</color>
(<color=#3366CC>Judaism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>) originated and have their holiest sites in the Middle East.
Most parts of the Middle East exhibit a hot and arid climate, especially in the Arabian and Egyptian regions. However, a
number of major rivers provide irrigation to support agriculture in certain areas, such as the <color=#3366CC>Nile</color> in Egypt, the Tigris and
the Euphrates in Mesopotamia, and the <color=#3366CC>Jordan River</color> in the Levant. Conversely, the Levantine coast and most of
Turkey collectively boast a relatively temperate <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean climate</color>, which yields dry summers with cool and wet
winters. A group of Middle Eastern countries that are located along the <color=#3366CC>Persian Gulf</color>—commonly called the Gulf Arab
states—have vast reserves of petroleum, which has served as a critical economic resource and accordingly influenced
regional politics. Owing to the Middle East's aridity and pervasive dependence on the <color=#3366CC>fossil fuel industry</color>, it is one of the
most vulnerable regions to <color=#3366CC>climate change</color> and water scarcity.
Terminology
The term "Middle East" may have originated with the India Office of the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color> in the 1850s. However, it
became more widely known through the <color=#3366CC>United States</color>, particularly after American naval strategist <color=#3366CC>Alfred Thayer Mahan</color>
used the term to "designate the area between <color=#3366CC>Arabia</color> and <color=#3366CC>India</color>" in 1902. During this period, the United Kingdom was
vying for influence in <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color> as part of the "<color=#3366CC>Great Game</color>" against the <color=#3366CC>Russian Empire</color>, which was in the process of
<color=#3366CC>conquering the entire region</color>.
Realizing the "Middle East" to be a region of immense strategic value centred around the <color=#3366CC>Persian Gulf</color>, Mahan took the
view that, beyond the <color=#3366CC>Suez Canal</color> in British-ruled Egypt, the Persian Gulf was the most important passage for the
United Kingdom in the context of keeping in check any possible Russian advance towards <color=#3366CC>British-ruled India</color>. Mahan
first used the term in his September 1902 article "The Persian Gulf and International Relations" for the British journal
National Review in <color=#3366CC>London</color>.
The Middle East, if I may adopt a term which I have not seen, will some day need its Malta, as well as its Gibraltar; it
does not follow that either will be in the Persian Gulf. Naval force has the quality of mobility which carries with it the
privilege of temporary absences; but it needs to find on every scene of operation established bases of refit, of supply,
and in case of disaster, of security. The <color=#3366CC>British Navy</color> should have the facility to concentrate in force if occasion arise,
about Aden, India, and the Persian Gulf.
Mahan's article was reprinted in the British newspaper <color=#3366CC>The Times</color> and followed by a 20-article series entitled "The
Middle Eastern Question" by British historian and diplomat Valentine Chirol. In this series, which began in October
1902, he would expand the definition of "Middle East" to include "those regions of Asia which extend to the borders of
India or command the approaches to India." After the series ended in 1903, The Times removed quotation marks from
subsequent uses of the term.
Until <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>, it was customary to refer to areas centred on <color=#3366CC>Turkey</color> and the Eastern Mediterranean as the "<color=#3366CC>Near</color>

<color=#3366CC>East</color>" in juxtaposition with the "<color=#3366CC>Far East</color>" centred on <color=#3366CC>China</color>, India, and <color=#3366CC>Japan</color>. The Middle East was then defined as the
area from <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color> to <color=#3366CC>Burma</color>—namely, the area between the Near East and the Far East—which now broadly
corresponds with <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color>.
In the late 1930s, the <color=#3366CC>Cairo</color>-based Middle East Command was established for the <color=#3366CC>British Armed Forces</color>. After that time,
the term "Middle East" gained broader usage across both Europe and the United States. The Middle East Institute, for
example, was founded in <color=#3366CC>Washington, D.C.</color> in 1946.
While "<color=#3366CC>Southwest Asia</color>" or "Swasia" have been presented sparsely as alternatives, the inclusion of Egypt (located
entirely in <color=#3366CC>North Africa</color> except for the <color=#3366CC>Sinai Peninsula</color>) among those countries that are counted as part of the Middle
East challenges the usefulness of such terms. Furthermore, the core term "Asia" itself is <color=#3366CC>Eurocentric</color>, having been
expanded upon from a term coined by the <color=#3366CC>ancient Greeks</color> to refer to contemporary Anatolia.
Usage and criticism
The description Middle has also led to some confusion over changing definitions. Before the <color=#3366CC>First World War</color>, "Near
East" was used in English to refer to the <color=#3366CC>Balkans</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color>, while "Middle East" referred to the

<color=#3366CC>Caucasus</color>, <color=#3366CC>Persia</color>, and Arabian lands, and sometimes <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color>, <color=#3366CC>India</color> and others. In contrast, "<color=#3366CC>Far East</color>" referred to
the countries of <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color> (e.g. <color=#3366CC>China</color>, <color=#3366CC>Japan</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Korea</color>).
With the collapse of the Ottoman Empire in 1918, "Near East" largely fell out of common use in English, while "Middle
East" came to be applied to the emerging independent countries of the <color=#3366CC>Islamic world</color>. However, the usage "Near East"
was retained by a variety of academic disciplines, including <color=#3366CC>archaeology</color> and <color=#3366CC>ancient history</color>. In their usage, the term
describes an area identical to the term Middle East, which is not used by these disciplines (see <color=#3366CC>ancient Near East</color>).
The first official use of the term "Middle East" by the <color=#3366CC>United States government</color> was in the 1957 Eisenhower Doctrine,
which pertained to the <color=#3366CC>Suez Crisis</color>. Secretary of State <color=#3366CC>John Foster Dulles</color> defined the Middle East as "the area lying

between and including <color=#3366CC>Libya</color> on the west and <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color> on the east, <color=#3366CC>Syria</color> and <color=#3366CC>Iraq</color> on the North and the Arabian
peninsula to the south, plus the <color=#3366CC>Sudan</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ethiopia</color>." In 1958, the <color=#3366CC>State Department</color> explained that the terms "Near
East" and "Middle East" were interchangeable, and defined the region as including only <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>, Syria, <color=#3366CC>Israel</color>, <color=#3366CC>Lebanon</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Jordan</color>, Iraq, <color=#3366CC>Saudi Arabia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kuwait</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bahrain</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Qatar</color>.
Since the late 20th century, scholars and journalists from the region, such as journalist Louay Khraish and historian
Hassan Hanafi have criticized the use of "Middle East" as a <color=#3366CC>Eurocentric</color> and <color=#3366CC>colonialist</color> term.
The <color=#3366CC>Associated Press</color> Stylebook of 2004 says that Near East formerly referred to the farther west countries while
Middle East referred to the eastern ones, but that now they are synonymous. It instructs:
Use Middle East unless Near East is used by a source in a story. Mideast is also acceptable, but Middle East is
preferred.
Translations
European languages have adopted terms similar to Near East and Middle East. Since these are based on a relative
description, the meanings depend on the country and are generally different from the English terms. In <color=#3366CC>German</color> the
term (Near East) is still in common use (nowadays the term Mittlerer Osten is more and more common in press texts
translated from English sources, albeit having a distinct meaning).

In Slavic languages like <color=#3366CC>Russian</color> (Blizhniy Vostok), <color=#3366CC>Bulgarian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Polish</color> Bliski Wschód or <color=#3366CC>Croatian</color> Bliski istok, (terms
meaning Near East are the only appropriate ones for the region).

However, some European languages do have "Middle East" equivalents, such as <color=#3366CC>French</color>, <color=#3366CC>Swedish</color>, <color=#3366CC>Spanish</color>, <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> is
(Mesi Anatoli), and <color=#3366CC>Italian</color>.
Perhaps because of the political influence of the United States and Europe, and the prominence of Western press, the
Arabic equivalent of Middle East (Arabic: ash-Sharq al-Awsat) has become standard usage in the mainstream Arabic
press. It comprises the same meaning as the term "Middle East" in North American and Western European usage. The
designation, Mashriq, also from the Arabic root for East, also denotes a variously defined region around the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>, the
eastern part of the Arabic-speaking world (as opposed to the <color=#3366CC>Maghreb</color>, the western part). Even though the term
originated in the West, countries of the Middle East that use languages other than Arabic also use that term in
translation. For instance, the <color=#3366CC>Persian</color> equivalent for Middle East is (Khāvar-e miyāneh), the Hebrew is (hamizrach
hatikhon), and the Turkish is Orta Doğu.
Countries and territories
Common definition of the Middle East

Traditionally included within the Middle East are <color=#3366CC>Arabia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Asia Minor</color>, <color=#3366CC>East Thrace</color>, <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>, <color=#3366CC>Iran</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color>, and the Socotra Archipelago. The region includes 17 <color=#3366CC>UN</color>-recognized countries and one <color=#3366CC>British Overseas</color>
<color=#3366CC>Territory</color>.
a. <color=#3366CC>Jerusalem</color> is the proclaimed capital of Israel, which is disputed, and the actual location of the Knesset, Israeli
Supreme Court, and other governmental institutions of Israel. <color=#3366CC>Ramallah</color> is the actual location of the government of
Palestine, whereas the proclaimed capital of Palestine is <color=#3366CC>East Jerusalem</color>, which is disputed. b. Controlled by the
Houthis due to the <color=#3366CC>ongoing civil war</color>. Seat of government moved to Aden.
Other definitions of the Middle East
Various concepts are often paralleled to the Middle East, most notably the <color=#3366CC>Near East</color>, <color=#3366CC>Fertile Crescent</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>.
These are geographical concepts, which refer to large sections of the modern-day Middle East, with the Near East
being the closest to the Middle East in its geographical meaning. Due to it primarily being Arabic speaking, the
<color=#3366CC>Maghreb</color> region of North Africa is sometimes included.
"Greater Middle East" is a <color=#3366CC>political</color> term coined by the second Bush administration in the first decade of the 21st century

to denote various countries, pertaining to the <color=#3366CC>Muslim world</color>, specifically <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Iran</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Turkey</color>.
Various <color=#3366CC>Central Asian</color> countries are sometimes also included.
History

The Middle East lies at the juncture of <color=#3366CC>Africa</color> and <color=#3366CC>Eurasia</color> and of the <color=#3366CC>Indian Ocean</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color> (see

also: Indo-Mediterranean). It is the birthplace and <color=#3366CC>spiritual</color> center of religions such as <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>, <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, <color=#3366CC>Judaism</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Manichaeism</color>, Yezidi, <color=#3366CC>Druze</color>, Yarsan, and <color=#3366CC>Mandeanism</color>, and in Iran, <color=#3366CC>Mithraism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Zoroastrianism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Manicheanism</color>, and the
<color=#3366CC>Baháí Faith</color>. Throughout its history the Middle East has been a major center of world affairs; a strategically,
economically, politically, culturally, and religiously sensitive area. The region is one of the regions where agriculture
was independently discovered, and from the Middle East it was spread, during the Neolithic, to different regions of the
world such as Europe, the Indus Valley and Eastern Africa.
Prior to the formation of civilizations, advanced cultures formed all over the Middle East during the <color=#3366CC>Stone Age</color>. The
search for agricultural lands by agriculturalists, and pastoral lands by herdsmen meant different migrations took place
within the region and shaped its ethnic and demographic makeup.
The Middle East is widely and most famously known as the <color=#3366CC>cradle of civilization</color>. The world's earliest civilizations,

<color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color> (<color=#3366CC>Sumer</color>, <color=#3366CC>Akkad</color>, <color=#3366CC>Assyria</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Babylonia</color>), <color=#3366CC>ancient Egypt</color> and Kish in the Levant, all originated in the Fertile
Crescent and <color=#3366CC>Nile</color> Valley regions of the ancient Near East. These were followed by the <color=#3366CC>Hittite</color>, Greek, <color=#3366CC>Hurrian</color> and

Urartian civilisations of <color=#3366CC>Asia Minor</color>; <color=#3366CC>Elam</color>, <color=#3366CC>Persia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Median</color> civilizations in <color=#3366CC>Iran</color>, as well as the civilizations of the

<color=#3366CC>Levant</color> (such as <color=#3366CC>Ebla</color>, Mari, Nagar, <color=#3366CC>Ugarit</color>, <color=#3366CC>Canaan</color>, Aramea, <color=#3366CC>Mitanni</color>, <color=#3366CC>Phoenicia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Israel</color>) and the <color=#3366CC>Arabian Peninsula</color>
(Magan, <color=#3366CC>Sheba</color>, Ubar). The Near East was first largely unified under the <color=#3366CC>Neo Assyrian Empire</color>, then the <color=#3366CC>Achaemenid</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color> followed later by the <color=#3366CC>Macedonian Empire</color> and after this to some degree by the Iranian empires (namely the

<color=#3366CC>Parthian</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sasanian Empires</color>), the <color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color>. The region served as the intellectual
and economic center of the Roman Empire and played an exceptionally important role due to its periphery on the
Sasanian Empire. Thus, the <color=#3366CC>Romans</color> stationed up to five or six of their legions in the region for the sole purpose of
defending it from Sasanian and Bedouin raids and invasions.
From the 4th century CE onward, the Middle East became the center of the two main powers at the time, the Byzantine
Empire and the Sasanian Empire. However, it would be the later <color=#3366CC>Islamic Caliphates</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>, or <color=#3366CC>Islamic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Golden Age</color> which began with the <color=#3366CC>Islamic conquest</color> of the region in the 7th century AD, that would first unify the entire
Middle East as a distinct region and create the dominant <color=#3366CC>Islamic</color> <color=#3366CC>Arab</color> ethnic identity that largely (but not exclusively)
persists today. The 4 caliphates that dominated the Middle East for more than 600 years were the <color=#3366CC>Rashidun Caliphate</color>,

the <color=#3366CC>Umayyad Caliphate</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Abbasid Caliphate</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Fatimid Caliphate</color>. Additionally, the <color=#3366CC>Mongols</color> would come to
dominate the region, the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Armenia</color> would incorporate parts of the region to their domain, the <color=#3366CC>Seljuks</color> would
rule the region and spread Turko-Persian culture, and the <color=#3366CC>Franks</color> would found the <color=#3366CC>Crusader states</color> that would stand for
roughly two centuries. Josiah Russell estimates the population of what he calls "Islamic territory" as roughly 12.5 million
in 1000 – <color=#3366CC>Anatolia</color> 8 million, Syria 2 million, and <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color> 1.5 million. From the 16th century onward, the Middle East came
to be dominated, once again, by two main powers: the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color> and <color=#3366CC>Safavid Iran</color>.
The modern Middle East began after <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>, when the Ottoman Empire, which was allied with the <color=#3366CC>Central Powers</color>,
was defeated by the <color=#3366CC>Allies</color> and <color=#3366CC>partitioned</color> into a number of separate nations, initially under British and French
Mandates. Other defining events in this transformation included the establishment of Israel in 1948 and the eventual
departure of European powers, notably <color=#3366CC>Britain</color> and <color=#3366CC>France</color> by the end of the 1960s. They were supplanted in some part
by the rising influence of the United States from the 1970s onward.
In the 20th century, the region's significant stocks of <color=#3366CC>crude oil</color> gave it new strategic and economic importance. Mass
production of oil began around 1945, with Saudi Arabia, Iran, Kuwait, Iraq, and the <color=#3366CC>United Arab Emirates</color> having large
quantities of oil. Estimated oil reserves, especially in Saudi Arabia and Iran, are some of the highest in the world, and
the international oil cartel <color=#3366CC>OPEC</color> is dominated by Middle Eastern countries.
During the Cold War, the Middle East was a theater of ideological struggle between the two superpowers and their
allies: <color=#3366CC>NATO</color> and the United States on one side, and the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> and <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Pact</color> on the other, as they
competed to influence regional allies. Besides the political reasons there was also the "ideological conflict" between the
two systems. Moreover, as Louise Fawcett argues, among many important areas of contention, or perhaps more
accurately of anxiety, were, first, the desires of the superpowers to gain strategic advantage in the region, second, the
fact that the region contained some two-thirds of the world's oil reserves in a context where oil was becoming
increasingly vital to the economy of the Western world [...] Within this contextual framework, the United States sought
to divert the Arab world from Soviet influence. Throughout the 20th and 21st centuries, the region has experienced both
periods of relative peace and tolerance and periods of conflict particularly between <color=#3366CC>Sunnis</color> and <color=#3366CC>Shiites</color>.
Geography
Climate change
Economy
Middle Eastern economies range from being very poor (such as Gaza Strip and Yemen) to extremely wealthy nations
(such as Qatar and the United Arab Emirates). According to the <color=#3366CC>International Monetary Fund</color>, the three largest Middle
Eastern economies in nominal GDP in 2023 were Saudi Arabia ($1.06 trillion), Turkey ($1.03 trillion), and Israel ($0.54
trillion). For nominal GDP per person, the highest ranking countries are Qatar ($83,891), Israel ($55,535), the United
Arab Emirates ($49,451) and Cyprus ($33,807). Turkey ($3.6 trillion), Saudi Arabia ($2.3 trillion), and Iran ($1.7 trillion)
had the largest economies in terms of GDP PPP. For GDP PPP per person, the highest-ranking countries are Qatar
($124,834), the United Arab Emirates ($88,221), Saudi Arabia ($64,836), Bahrain ($60,596) and Israel ($54,997). The
lowest-ranking country in the Middle East, in terms of GDP nominal per capita, is Yemen ($573).
The economic structure of Middle Eastern nations are different because while some are heavily dependent on export of
only oil and oil-related products (Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait), others have a highly diverse
economic base (such as Cyprus, Israel, Turkey and Egypt). Industries of the Middle Eastern region include oil and
oil-related products, agriculture, cotton, cattle, dairy, textiles, leather products, surgical instruments, defence equipment
(guns, ammunition, tanks, submarines, fighter jets, UAVs, and missiles). Banking is an important sector, especially for
United Arab Emirates and Bahrain.
With the exception of Cyprus, Turkey, Egypt, Lebanon and Israel, tourism has been a relatively undeveloped area of
the economy, in part because of the socially conservative nature of the region as well as political turmoil in certain
regions. Since the end of the COVID pandemic however, countries such as the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and
Jordan have begun attracting greater numbers of tourists because of improving tourist facilities and the relaxing of
tourism-related restrictive policies.
Unemployment is high in the Middle East and North Africa region, particularly among people aged 15–29, a
demographic representing 30% of the region's population. The total regional unemployment rate in 2025 is 10.8%, and
among youth is as high as 28%.
Demographics
Ethnic groups
<color=#3366CC>Arabs</color> constitute the largest ethnic group in the Middle East, followed by various Iranian peoples and then by <color=#3366CC>Turkic</color>
<color=#3366CC>peoples</color> (Turkish, Azeris, Syrian Turkmen, and Iraqi Turkmen). Native ethnic groups of the region include, in addition to

Arabs, Arameans, Assyrians, <color=#3366CC>Baloch</color>, <color=#3366CC>Berbers</color>, <color=#3366CC>Copts</color>, <color=#3366CC>Druze</color>, Greek Cypriots, <color=#3366CC>Jews</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kurds</color>, Lurs, Mandaeans,
<color=#3366CC>Persians</color>, Samaritans, Shabaks, Tats, and Zazas. European ethnic groups that form a diaspora in the region include
Albanians, Bosniaks, <color=#3366CC>Circassians</color> (including Kabardians), Crimean Tatars, Greeks, Franco-Levantines,
Italo-Levantines, and Iraqi Turkmens. Among other migrant populations are <color=#3366CC>Chinese</color>, Filipinos, Indians, Indonesians,
Pakistanis, <color=#3366CC>Pashtuns</color>, <color=#3366CC>Romani</color>, and Afro-Arabs.
Migration
"Migration has always provided an important vent for labor market pressures in the Middle East. For the period between
the 1970s and 1990s, the Arab states of the Persian Gulf in particular provided a rich source of employment for workers
from Egypt, Yemen and the countries of the Levant, while Europe had attracted young workers from North African
countries due both to proximity and the legacy of colonial ties between France and the majority of North African states."
According to the <color=#3366CC>International Organization for Migration</color>, there are 13 million first-generation migrants from <color=#3366CC>Arab</color>
<color=#3366CC>nations</color> in the world, of which 5.8 reside in other Arab countries. Expatriates from Arab countries contribute to the
circulation of financial and human capital in the region and thus significantly promote regional development. In 2009
Arab countries received a total of US$35.1 billion in remittance in-flows and remittances sent to <color=#3366CC>Jordan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>Lebanon</color> from other Arab countries are 40 to 190 per cent higher than trade revenues between these and other Arab
countries. In <color=#3366CC>Somalia</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Somali Civil War</color> has greatly increased the size of the Somali diaspora, as many of the best
educated Somalis left for Middle Eastern countries as well as <color=#3366CC>Europe</color> and <color=#3366CC>North America</color>.
Non-Arab Middle Eastern countries such as <color=#3366CC>Turkey</color>, <color=#3366CC>Israel</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Iran</color> are also subject to important migration dynamics.
A fair proportion of those migrating from Arab nations are from ethnic and religious minorities facing persecution and
are not necessarily ethnic Arabs, Iranians or Turks. Large numbers of <color=#3366CC>Kurds</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jews</color>, Assyrians, Greeks, and Armenians
as well as many Mandaeans have left nations such as Iraq, Iran, Syria and Turkey for these reasons during the last
century. In Iran, many religious minorities such as <color=#3366CC>Christians</color>, <color=#3366CC>Baháís</color>, Jews, and <color=#3366CC>Zoroastrians</color> have left since the
<color=#3366CC>Islamic Revolution of 1979</color>.
Languages
The six top languages, in terms of numbers of speakers, are Arabic, <color=#3366CC>Persian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Turkish</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kurdish</color>, Modern Hebrew and
Greek. About 20 minority languages are also spoken in the Middle East.
Arabic, with all its dialects, is the most widely spoken language in the Middle East, with <color=#3366CC>Literary Arabic</color> being official in
all North African and in most West Asian countries. Arabic dialects are also spoken in some adjacent areas in
neighbouring Middle Eastern non-Arab countries. It is a member of the <color=#3366CC>Semitic branch</color> of the Afro-Asiatic languages.
Several Modern South Arabian languages such as Mehri and Soqotri are also spoken in Yemen and Oman. Another
Semitic language is <color=#3366CC>Aramaic</color> and its dialects are spoken mainly by Assyrians and Mandaeans, with Western Aramaic
still spoken in two villages near Damascus, Syria. There is also an <color=#3366CC>Oasis Berber</color>-speaking community in Egypt where
the language is also known as Siwa. It is a non-Semitic Afro-Asiatic sister language.
<color=#3366CC>Persian</color> is the second most spoken language. While it is primarily spoken in <color=#3366CC>Iran</color> and some border areas in
neighbouring countries, the country is one of the region's largest and most populous. It belongs to the Indo-Iranian
branch of the family of <color=#3366CC>Indo-European languages</color>. Other Western Iranic languages spoken in the region include
Achomi, Daylami, <color=#3366CC>Kurdish</color> dialects, Semmani, Lurish, amongst many others.
The close third-most widely spoken language, <color=#3366CC>Turkish</color>, is largely confined to Turkey, which is also one of the region's
largest and most populous countries, but it is present in areas in neighboring countries. It is a member of the <color=#3366CC>Turkic</color>
<color=#3366CC>languages</color>, which have their origins in East Asia. Another Turkic language, <color=#3366CC>Azerbaijani</color>, is spoken by Azerbaijanis in
Iran.
The fourth-most widely spoken language, <color=#3366CC>Kurdish</color>, is spoken in the countries of Iran, Iraq, Syria, and Turkey, <color=#3366CC>Sorani</color>
<color=#3366CC>Kurdish</color> is the second official language in Iraq (instated after the 2005 constitution) after Arabic.
Hebrew is the official language of <color=#3366CC>Israel</color>, with Arabic given a special status after the 2018 Basic law lowered its status
from an official language prior to 2018. Hebrew is spoken and used by over 80% of Israel's population, the other 20%
using Arabic. Modern Hebrew only began being spoken in the 20th century after being revived in the late 19th century
by Elizer Ben-Yehuda (Elizer Perlman) and European Jewish settlers, with the first native Hebrew speaker being born
Greek is one of the two official languages of <color=#3366CC>Cyprus</color>, and the country's main language. Small communities of Greek
speakers exist all around the Middle East; until the 20th century it was also widely spoken in Asia Minor (being the
second most spoken language there, after Turkish) and Egypt. During the antiquity, <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greek</color> was the <color=#3366CC>lingua</color>
<color=#3366CC>franca</color> for many areas of the western Middle East and until the Muslim expansion it was widely spoken there as well.
Until the late 11th century, it was also the main spoken language in <color=#3366CC>Asia Minor</color>; after that it was gradually replaced by
the Turkish language as the Anatolian Turks expanded and the local Greeks were assimilated, especially in the interior.
<color=#3366CC>English</color> is one of the official languages of Akrotiri and Dhekelia. It is also commonly taught and used as a foreign

second language, in countries such as <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jordan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Iran</color>, <color=#3366CC>Iraq</color>, <color=#3366CC>Qatar</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bahrain</color>, <color=#3366CC>United Arab Emirates</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Kuwait</color>. It is
also a main language in some Emirates of the United Arab Emirates. It is also spoken as native language by Jewish
immigrants from Anglophone countries (UK, US, Australia) in Israel and understood widely as second language there.
<color=#3366CC>French</color> is taught and used in many government facilities and media in <color=#3366CC>Lebanon</color>, and is taught in some primary and
secondary schools of <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color> and <color=#3366CC>Syria</color>. <color=#3366CC>Maltese</color>, a Semitic language mainly spoken in Europe, is used by the
Franco-Maltese diaspora in Egypt. Due to widespread immigration of French Jews to Israel, it is the native language of
approximately 200,000 Jews in Israel.
<color=#3366CC>Armenian</color> speakers are to be found in the region. <color=#3366CC>Georgian</color> is spoken by the Georgian diaspora.
<color=#3366CC>Russian</color> is spoken by a large portion of the Israeli population, because of emigration in the late 1990s. Russian today is
a popular unofficial language in use in <color=#3366CC>Israel</color>; news, radio and sign boards can be found in Russian around the country
after Hebrew and Arabic. Circassian is also spoken by the diaspora in the region and by almost all Circassians in Israel
who speak Hebrew and English as well.
The largest <color=#3366CC>Romanian</color>-speaking community in the Middle East is found in <color=#3366CC>Israel</color>, where As of 1995 Romanian is spoken
by 5% of the population.
<color=#3366CC>Bengali</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hindi</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Urdu</color> are widely spoken by migrant communities in many Middle Eastern countries, such as Saudi
Arabia (where 20–25% of the population is South Asian), the United Arab Emirates (where 50–55% of the population is
South Asian), and Qatar, which have large numbers of <color=#3366CC>Pakistani</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bangladeshi</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Indian</color> immigrants.
Religion
The Middle East is very diverse when it comes to religions, many of which originated there. <color=#3366CC>Islam</color> is the largest religion
in the Middle East, but other faiths that originated there, such as <color=#3366CC>Judaism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>, are also well represented.
Christian communities have played a vital role in the Middle East, and they represent 78% of <color=#3366CC>Cyprus</color> population, and
40.5% of <color=#3366CC>Lebanon</color>, where the Lebanese president, half of the cabinet, and half of the parliament follow one of the
various Lebanese Christian rites. There are also important minority religions like the <color=#3366CC>Baháí Faith</color>, Yarsanism, Yazidism,
<color=#3366CC>Zoroastrianism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mandaeism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Druze</color>, and Shabakism, and in ancient times the region was home to <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamian</color>

<color=#3366CC>religions</color>, <color=#3366CC>Canaanite religions</color>, <color=#3366CC>Manichaeism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mithraism</color> and various <color=#3366CC>monotheist</color> <color=#3366CC>gnostic</color> sects.
Culture
Sport
The Middle East has recently become more prominent in hosting global sport events due to its wealth and desire to
diversify its economy.
The South Asian diaspora is a major backer of <color=#3366CC>cricket</color> in the region.
Bangkok
Bangkok, known in Thai as Krung Thep Maha Nakhon and colloquially as Krung Thep, is the <color=#3366CC>capital</color> and largest city of
the Kingdom of <color=#3366CC>Thailand</color>. The city occupies 1568.7 km2 in the <color=#3366CC>Chao Phraya River</color> delta in <color=#3366CC>central Thailand</color> and has an
estimated population of 9.1 million people as of 2024, 15.9% of the country's population. Over 17.4 million people (25%
of Thailand's population) live within the surrounding Bangkok Metropolitan Region as of the 2021 estimate, making
Bangkok a <color=#3366CC>megacity</color> and an extreme <color=#3366CC>primate city</color>, dwarfing Thailand's other urban centres in both size and importance
to the national economy.
Bangkok traces its roots to a small trading post during the <color=#3366CC>Ayutthaya era</color> in the 15th century, which eventually grew and
became the site of two capital cities, Thonburi in 1767 and <color=#3366CC>Rattanakosin</color> in 1782. Bangkok was at the heart of the
modernization of Siam during the late 19th century, as the country faced pressures from the West. The city was at the
centre of the country's political struggles throughout the 20th century, as Siam—later renamed Thailand—abolished
absolute monarchy, adopted constitutional rule, and underwent numerous coups and several uprisings. The city, which
was incorporated as a special administrative area under the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration in 1972, grew rapidly
during the 1960s through the 1980s and now exerts a significant impact on Thailand's politics, economy, education,
media, and modern society.
The Asian investment boom in the 1980s and 1990s led many multinational corporations to locate their regional
headquarters in Bangkok. The city is now a regional force in finance, business, and pop culture. It is an international
hub for transport and health care, and has emerged as a centre for the arts, fashion, and entertainment. The city is
known for its street life and cultural landmarks, as well as its <color=#3366CC>red-light districts</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Grand Palace</color> and <color=#3366CC>Buddhist</color>
<color=#3366CC>temples</color>, including Wat Arun and Wat Pho, stand in contrast with other tourist attractions such as the nightlife scenes of
Khaosan Road and Patpong. Bangkok is among the world's top tourist destinations and has been named the world's
most visited city in several international rankings.
Bangkok's rapid growth, coupled with little <color=#3366CC>urban planning</color>, has resulted in a haphazard cityscape and inadequate
infrastructure. Despite an extensive expressway network, an inadequate road network and substantial private car
usage have led to chronic and crippling <color=#3366CC>traffic congestion</color>, which caused severe <color=#3366CC>air pollution</color> in the 1990s. The city has
since turned to public transport to solve the problem, operating 10 urban rail lines and building other public transit;
however, congestion remains a prevalent issue.
History
<color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Ayutthaya</color> 15th century – 1767 Kingdom of Thonburi 1767–1782 <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Siam</color> 1782–1932 <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Thailand</color> 1932–present
The history of Bangkok dates at least back to the early 15th century, to when it was a village on the west bank of the
<color=#3366CC>Chao Phraya River</color>, under the rule of <color=#3366CC>Ayutthaya</color>. Because of its strategic location near the mouth of the river, the town
gradually increased in importance. Bangkok initially served as a customs outpost with forts on both sides of the river,
and was the site of a siege in 1688, in which the French were expelled from Siam. After the fall of Ayutthaya to the
<color=#3366CC>Burmese</color> in 1767, the newly crowned King <color=#3366CC>Taksin</color> established his capital at the town, which became the base of the
Thonburi Kingdom. In 1782, King <color=#3366CC>Phutthayotfa Chulalok</color> (Rama I) succeeded Taksin, moved the capital to the eastern
bank's Rattanakosin Island, thus founding the <color=#3366CC>Rattanakosin Kingdom</color>. The City Pillar was erected on 21 April 1782,
which is regarded as the date of the foundation of Bangkok as the capital.
Bangkok's economy gradually expanded through international trade, first with <color=#3366CC>China</color>, then with Western merchants
returning in the early to mid-19th century. As the capital, Bangkok was the centre of Siam's modernization as it faced
pressure from Western powers in the late 19th century. The reigns of Kings <color=#3366CC>Mongkut</color> (Rama IV, r. 1851–68) and
<color=#3366CC>Chulalongkorn</color> (Rama V, r. 1868–1910) saw the introduction of the steam engine, printing press, rail transport and
utilities infrastructure in the city, as well as formal education and healthcare. Bangkok became the centre stage for
power struggles between the military and political elite as the country abolished absolute monarchy in 1932.
As <color=#3366CC>Thailand</color> allied with Japan in World War II, Bangkok was subjected to Allied bombing, but rapidly grew in the
post-war period as a result of US aid and government-sponsored investment. Bangkok's role as a US military R&R
destination boosted its tourism industry, as well as firmly establishing it as a sex tourism destination. Disproportionate
urban development led to increasing income inequalities and migration from rural areas into Bangkok; its population
surged from 1.8 million to 3 million in the 1960s.
Following the US withdrawal from <color=#3366CC>Vietnam</color> in 1973, Japanese businesses took over as leaders in investment, and the
expansion of export-oriented manufacturing led to the growth of the financial market in Bangkok. Rapid growth of the
city continued through the 1980s and early 1990s, until it was stalled by the <color=#3366CC>1997 Asian financial crisis</color>. By then, many
public and social issues had emerged, among them the strain on infrastructure reflected in the city's notorious traffic
jams. Bangkok's role as the nation's political stage continues to be seen in strings of popular protests, from the student
uprisings in 1973 and 1976, anti-military demonstrations in 1992, and frequent street protests since 2006, including
those by groups opposing and supporting former prime minister <color=#3366CC>Thaksin Shinawatra</color> from 2006 to 2013, and a renewed
student-led movement in 2020.
Administration of the city was first formalized by King Chulalongkorn in 1906, with the establishment of Monthon Krung
Thep Phra Maha Nakhon as a national subdivision. In 1915, the monthon was split into several provinces, the
administrative boundaries of which have since further changed. The city in its current form was created in 1972 with the
formation of the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA), following the merger of Phra Nakhon province on the
eastern bank of the Chao Phraya and Thonburi province on the west during the previous year.
Name
The origin of the name Bangkok (pronounced in Thai as ) is unclear. Bang is a Thai word meaning 'a village on a
stream', and the name might have been derived from Bang Ko, ko meaning 'island', stemming from the city's watery
landscape. Another theory suggests that it is shortened from Bang Makok, makok being the name of Elaeocarpus
hygrophilus, a plant bearing olive-like fruit. This is supported by the former name of Wat Arun, a historic temple in the
area, that used to be called Wat Makok.
Officially, the town was known as Thonburi Si Mahasamut (from <color=#3366CC>Pali</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sanskrit</color>, literally 'city of treasures gracing the
ocean') or Thonburi, according to the <color=#3366CC>Ayutthaya Chronicles</color>. Bangkok was likely a colloquial name, albeit one widely
adopted by foreign visitors, who continued to use it to refer to the city even after the new capital's establishment.
When King <color=#3366CC>Rama I</color> established his new capital on the river's eastern bank, the city inherited Ayutthaya's ceremonial
name, of which there were many variants, including Krung Thep Thawarawadi Si Ayutthaya and Krung Thep Maha
Nakhon Si Ayutthaya. Edmund Roberts, visiting the city as envoy of the United States in 1833, noted that the city, since
becoming capital, was known as Sia-Yut'hia, and this is the name used in international treaties of the period.
The city's ceremonial name came into use during the reign of King <color=#3366CC>Mongkut</color>. The full name reads as follows:
Krung Thep Maha Nakhon Amon Rattanakosin Mahintharayutthaya Mahadilok Phop Noppharat Ratchathani Burirom
Udomratchaniwet Mahasathan Amon Phiman Awatan Sathit Sakkathattiya Witsanukam Prasit
The name, composed of <color=#3366CC>Pali</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sanskrit</color> root words, translates as:
The city of angels, great city of immortals, magnificent city of the Nine Gems, seat of the King, city of royal palaces,
home of gods incarnate, erected by Vishvakarman at <color=#3366CC>Indra</color>'s behest.
The name is listed in <color=#3366CC>Guinness World Records</color> as the world's longest place name at 168 letters. Many Thais who recall
the full name do so because of its use in the 1989 song "Krung Thep Maha Nakhon" by Thai rock band
Asanee–Wasan, the lyrics of which consist entirely of the city's full name, repeated throughout the song.
Today, the city is officially known in Thai by a shortened form of the full ceremonial name, Krung Thep Maha Nakhon,
which is colloquially further shortened to Krung Thep or the initialism Ko Tho Mo (.). Krung is a Thai word of <color=#3366CC>Khmer</color>
origin, meaning 'capital, king', while thep, is from Pali/Sanskrit deva, meaning 'deity' or 'god'. The name is more
commonly translated as 'City of Angels', which is also used to draw comparisons with Los Angeles in the United States,
a comparably sized city with similar traffic issues. Another nickname sometimes used to refer to the city is The Big
Mango, a tongue-in-cheek comparison to The Big Apple for New York City.
Government
The city of Bangkok is locally governed by the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA). Although its boundaries are
at the provincial (changwat) level, unlike the other 76 provinces, Bangkok is a special administrative area whose
governor is directly elected to serve a four-year term. The governor, together with four appointed deputies, forms the
executive body, which implements policies through the BMA civil service headed by the Permanent Secretary for the
BMA. In separate elections, each district elects one or more city councillors, who form the Bangkok Metropolitan
Council. The council is the BMA's legislative body and has power over municipal ordinances and the city's budget. The
first gubernatorial election in nine years took place on 22 May 2022 after an extended lapse following the 2014 Thai
coup d'état, and was won by Chadchart Sittipunt., then again on 28 June 2026 for a second term in office.
Bangkok is divided into fifty districts (khet, equivalent to amphoe in the other provinces), which are further subdivided
into 180 sub-districts (khwaeng, equivalent to tambon). Each district is managed by a district director appointed by the
governor. District councils, elected to four-year terms, serve as advisory bodies to their respective district directors.
The BMA is divided into sixteen departments, each overseeing different aspects of the administration's responsibilities.
Most of these responsibilities concern the city's infrastructure, and include city planning, building control, transportation,
drainage, waste management, and city beautification, as well as education, medical, and rescue services. Many of
these services are provided jointly with other agencies. The BMA has the authority to implement local ordinances,
although civil law enforcement falls under the jurisdiction of the Metropolitan Police Bureau.
As the capital of Thailand, Bangkok is the seat of all branches of the national government. The Government House,
Parliament House, and Supreme, Administrative, and Constitutional Courts are all in the city. Sappaya-Sapasathan is
the largest parliament building in the world. The National Assembly of Thailand convenes there. Bangkok is the site of
the <color=#3366CC>Grand Palace</color> and Dusit Palace, respectively the official and de facto residence of the king. Most government
ministries also have headquarters and offices in the capital.
Symbols
The city seal shows <color=#3366CC>Hindu</color> god <color=#3366CC>Indra</color> riding in the clouds on Airavata, a divine white elephant known in Thai as Erawan.
In his hand Indra holds his weapon, the vajra. The seal is based on a painting done by Prince Naris, a brother of King
Chulalongkorn. The tree symbol of Bangkok is Ficus benjamina. Giant barb (Catlocarpio siamensis) has been chosen
as the aquatic animal of Bangkok. The official city slogan, adopted in 2012, reads:
As built by deities, the administrative centre, dazzling palaces and temples, the capital of Thailand
Geography
Bangkok covers an area of 1568.7 km2, ranking 69th among the other 76 provinces of Thailand. Of this, about 700 km2
forms the built-up urban area. It is ranked 73rd in the world in terms of land area. The city's <color=#3366CC>urban sprawl</color> reaches into
parts of the six other provinces that it borders, namely, in clockwise order from northwest: Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani,
Chachoengsao, Samut Prakan, Samut Sakhon, and Nakhon Pathom. Except for Chachoengsao, these provinces,
together with Bangkok, form the greater Bangkok Metropolitan Region.
Topography
Bangkok is situated in the Chao Phraya River delta in Thailand's <color=#3366CC>central plain</color>. The river meanders through the city in a
southerly direction, emptying into the <color=#3366CC>Gulf of Thailand</color> approximately 25 km south of the city centre. The area is flat and
low-lying, with an average elevation of 1.5 m <color=#3366CC>above sea level</color>. Most of the area was originally <color=#3366CC>swampland</color>, which was
gradually drained and irrigated for agriculture by the construction of canals (khlong) which took place from the 16th to
19th centuries. The course of the river as it flows through Bangkok has been modified by the construction of <color=#3366CC>several</color>
<color=#3366CC>shortcut canals</color>.
The city's waterway network served as the primary means of transport until the late 19th century, when modern roads
began to be built. Up until then, most people lived near or on the water, leading the city to be known during the 19th
century as the "<color=#3366CC>Venice</color> of the East". Many of these canals have since been filled in or paved over, but others still
crisscross the city, serving as major drainage channels and transport routes. Most canals are now badly polluted,
although the BMA has committed to the treatment and cleaning up of several canals.
The geology of the Bangkok area is characterised by a top layer of soft marine clay, known as "Bangkok clay",
averaging 15 m in thickness, which overlies an <color=#3366CC>aquifer</color> system consisting of eight known units. This feature has
contributed to the effects of <color=#3366CC>subsidence</color> caused by extensive groundwater pumping. First discovered in the 1970s,
subsidence soon became a critical issue, reaching a rate of 120 mm per year in 1981. Ground water management and
mitigation measures have since lessened the severity of the situation, and the rate of subsidence decreased to 10 to 30
mm per year in the early 2000s, though parts of the city are now 1 m below sea level.
Subsidence has resulted in increased flood risk, as Bangkok is already prone to flooding due to its low elevation and an
inadequate drainage infrastructure, often compounded by blockage from rubbish pollution (especially plastic waste).
The city now relies on flood barriers and augmenting drainage from canals by pumping and building drain tunnels, but
parts of Bangkok and its suburbs are still regularly inundated. Heavy downpours resulting in urban runoff overwhelming
drainage systems, and runoff discharge from upstream areas, are major triggering factors. Severe flooding affecting
much of the city occurred in 1995 and 2011. In 2011, most of Bangkok's northern, eastern, and western districts were
flooded, in some places for over two months.
Bangkok's geology also makes its tall buildings vulnerable to powerful earthquakes from far away, despite not being in
a seismically active area, as the clay layer has an amplifying effect on long-period ground motion, which tends to match
the <color=#3366CC>resonant frequency</color> of high-rises. Occupants of skyscrapers in Bangkok have often felt effects from earthquakes
centred hundreds of kilometres away in <color=#3366CC>northern Thailand</color> and Myanmar. Seismic considerations were only added to
the building code in 2007, making older structures particularly at risk.
Its coastal location makes Bangkok particularly vulnerable to <color=#3366CC>rising sea levels</color> due to <color=#3366CC>global warming</color> and climate
change. A study by the <color=#3366CC>OECD</color> has estimated that 5.138 million people in Bangkok may be exposed to coastal flooding
by 2070, the seventh highest figure among the world's port cities. There are fears that the city may be submerged by
2030. A study published in October 2019 in Nature Communications corrected earlier models of coastal elevations and
concluded that up to 12 million Thais—mostly in the greater Bangkok metropolitan area—face the prospect of annual
flooding events. This is compounded by coastal erosion, which is an issue in the gulf coastal area, a small length of
which lies within Bangkok's Bang Khun Thian District. Tidal flat ecosystems existed on the coast; however, many have
been reclaimed for agriculture, aquaculture, and salt works.
The closest mountain range to Bangkok is the Khao Khiao Massif, about 40 km southeast of the city. Phu Khao Thong,
the only hill in the metropolitan area, originated with a very large chedi that King <color=#3366CC>Rama III</color> (1787–1851) built at Wat
Saket. The chedi collapsed during construction because the soft soil could not support its weight. Over the next few
decades, the abandoned mud-and-brick structure acquired the shape of a natural hill and became overgrown with
weeds. The locals called it phu khao, as if it were a natural feature. In the 1940s, enclosing concrete walls were added
to stop the hill from eroding.
Climate
Like most of Thailand, Bangkok has a <color=#3366CC>tropical savanna climate</color> (Aw) under the <color=#3366CC>Köppen climate classification</color> and is
under the influence of the <color=#3366CC>Asian monsoon</color> system. The city experiences three seasons: hot, rainy, and cool, although
temperatures are fairly hot year-round, ranging from an average low of 23.2 C in December to an average high of 35.7
C in April. The annual average temperature is 28.9 C. The rainy season begins with the arrival of the southwest
<color=#3366CC>monsoon</color> around mid-May. September is the wettest month, with an average rainfall of 335.9 mm. The rainy season
lasts until October, when the dry and cool northeast monsoon takes over until February. The hot season is generally
dry, but it also sees occasional summer storms. The surface magnitude of Bangkok's <color=#3366CC>urban heat island</color> has been
measured at 2.5 C-change during the day and 8.0 C-change at night. The highest recorded temperature of Bangkok
metropolis was 41.0 C on 7 May 2023, and the lowest recorded temperature was 9.9 C in January 1955.
The Climate Impact Group at <color=#3366CC>NASA</color>'s Goddard Institute for Space Studies projected severe weather impacts on
Bangkok caused by <color=#3366CC>climate change</color>. It found that Bangkok in 1960 had 193 days at or above 32 °C. In 2018, Bangkok
can expect 276 days at or above 32 °C. The group forecasts a rise by 2100 to, on average, 297 to 344 days at or
above 32 °C.
